The question of whether antidepressants are more effective than placebo is genuinely contested, with major studies reaching opposing conclusions. On one side, a large Lancet meta-analysis of 522 randomized controlled trials (116,477 participants) found that all 21 commonly used antidepressants were more effective than placebo for treating acute depression in adults, with odds ratios ranging from 1.37 to 2.13 [d4][d5][d6]. The lead author described this as "the final answer to the controversy" [d1], and the findings were replicated across multiple reports of the same study [d3].

On the other side, a BMJ study analyzing FDA trial data from 73,388 participants found that the average drug-placebo difference was only 1.75 points on a depression rating scale, concluding that antidepressants are no better than placebo for approximately 85% of people, with only about 15% experiencing a meaningful drug-specific benefit [d2]. A Frontiers in Psychiatry article found "virtually no differences at all between drug and placebo among patients who had never been taken antidepressants before," suggesting antidepressants may work primarily through placebo mechanisms for first-time users [d7]. Scientific American similarly concluded that "the best available scientific evidence suggests that antidepressants do not work very well" when compared to placebo [d8], and an AAFP review noted that SSRIs and SNRIs "may not be more effective than placebo," with selective publication of positive studies having overstated their benefits [d9]. The NIMH-TDCRP trial also showed antidepressants and therapies "barely outperform placebo treatment" [d10].

In summary, while the Lancet meta-analysis provides the broadest evidence that antidepressants outperform placebo on average [d4][d5][d6], multiple other studies and analyses argue the difference is clinically marginal or limited to a minority of patients [d2][d7][d8][d9], leaving the debate unresolved.
